newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - short end set to rally.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - short end set to rally.

text.p: UK gilts should weather a blitz of domestic data this week, with the short end set to rally amid growing expectations that interest rates will remain on hold after Wednesday's monetary policy meeting, analysts said.
December unemployment, November average earnings data and December retail prices and PSBR figures -- should all help gilts to outperform jittery US Treasuries.
"All the data should be quite unchallenging," said BZW gilts analyst Kevin Adams.
The major focus for the gilt market will be Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George at around 1500 GMT on Wednesday.
Because the meeting is in the afternoon, any change in interest rates is unlikely to be announced until Thursday morning at around 0945 GMT.

The Bank has made it clear it believes interest rates should rise further from their present 6.0 percent level to prevent a resurgence of inflation, which is lodged stubbornly above the government's 2.5 percent target.

But anecdotal evidence of moderate pre-Christmas sales, softer than expected data on manufacturing output and Monday's subdued producer price data will lend weight to Clarke's present argument for keeping rates on hold.

"Clarke will be very reluctant to raise rates, and in that instance we will continue to see the gilt curve steepen," said Adams. "The short end will rally, leaving the long end vulnerable to a setback."
Some economists believe Clarke will delay any rate move until the next monetary policy meeting on Feb 5, by which time he will have seen preliminary Q4 GDP data due January 27.
"Clarke can afford not to raise rates now and he still has the option to put them up before the Bank's February inflation report," said Societe Generale analyst Tom Rayner.
"There's room for a rally at the short end on no rate change."
March short sterling futures were three basis points higher at 93.48 in early Monday trade, implying official interest rates of around 6.50 percent by the end of March.
Gilts kicked off the week in positive mood after a weaker than expected 0.5 percent rise in unadjusted output prices confirmed that pipeline inflationary pressures remain subdued.
The next report to catch the market's eye will be the British Retail Consortium's survey at 0030 GMT on Tuesday.
With strong consumer spending the main source of inflationary pressures, investors will look to the survey to confirm that pre-Christmas sales were robust but not booming.

December unemployment data on Wednesday will be keenly watched after last month's record 95,800 fall. According to a Reuter poll, economists expect it to fall by 30,000. Average earnings growth is seen stalled at 4.0 percent in November.
"It is only a matter of time before average earnings growth rises further, particularly given the tightness of the labour market," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr.
But he does not expect this to happen this month.
Economists expected December retail price data on Thursday to have a limited impact on the market as Clarke will know the data before he makes his decision on rates on Wednesday.
A Reuter poll suggests both headline and RPIX inflation edging down slightly at the end of last year.

Economists expect a 0.5 percent rise in the overall retail price index, giving a slight fall in the headline rate to 2.6 percent from 2.7 percent last month. Core inflation is seen slipping to 3.1 percent from a previous 3.3 percent.
The main risk of a correction for the market will come from the other side of the Atlantic this week as a barrage of U.S. data threatens to upset nervous Treasuries.
December retail sales and the consumer price index on Tuesday will be monitored after last Friday's strong payrolls data, as will industrial production data on Friday.
"I think it'll be a case of gilts outperforming U.S. Treasuries but not resisting any move altogether," said Adams.

He added there was little scope for substantial outperformance by gilts of the core European markets. "Even last week when we had some really good news for the market, the (gilt-Bund) spread didn't come in further than 183 basis points," Adams said.
The gilt-Bund spread at 10 years was 190 basis points in early Monday trade.
"The chances are we will trade over 200 in the near term...Whether we go there in the next week really depends on what the US data look like," Adams said.
